explanation: In the US, propping your feet up or letting the soles of your shoes face someone reads as very casual or overly relaxed rather than disrespectful - it's common to see people, including public figures, put their feet up to seem approachable. The main objection most Americans would have is practical (dirty shoes on furniture), not a belief that feet are symbolically unclean.
local_tip: Keep your feet on the floor in formal settings or around people you don't know well; it's fine to relax more with close friends or family.

also_check.note: Feet are considered the lowest, dirtiest part of the body; pointing soles at a person or a Buddha image is a serious insult.
Showing the soles of your feet or resting them on furniture is considered a genuine insult, not just casual.
Pointing your feet at someone, especially an elder or in a formal setting, is seen as poor manners, though a milder breach than in Thailand.

sources.title: 12 American Habits That Come Off as Rude Overseas
